text.title: Single Page Case Study Generation Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Single Page Case Study Generation application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The case study MUST fill all six slots in this order: problem (one to two sentences, the client's situation before the engagement), approach (two to three sentences naming the stack or method), outcome (one sentence with the headline number), numbers (the evidence list), pull-quote, and NDA indicator (named, anonymised, or full version on request). The whole document MUST fit on one page: at most 500 words plus at most one chart or screenshot. A missing slot or a second page is a rejected draft.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in B2B case-study writing (problem, solution, results structure); this methodology's six-slot definition

rule.rationale: Freelancers do not write case studies because there is no template and no stopping rule; a fixed slot list removes the blank page and the 500-word cap removes the endless draft. Prospects scan case studies inside a proposal pack in under a minute, so anything past one page is unread and anything that omits the problem slot reads as a feature list.

rule.statement: The numbers slot MUST contain at least one quantitative outcome written as baseline, final value and relative delta with its unit and measurement window (for example "p95 checkout 1,480 ms to 560 ms, minus 62 percent, 30 days before vs 30 days after"). "Significant improvement", a single number with no baseline, or a percentage with no absolute values MUST NOT appear in the slot.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in evidence-based marketing claims; FTC Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 255 (claims must be substantiated)

rule.rationale: Service-engagement case studies live or die on credible numbers, and SaaS-style templates fail freelance work because they assume product analytics exist. A delta without a baseline cannot be checked and a prospect who has been burned once discounts it to zero; a baseline, final and window can be asked about on the discovery call, which is where the case study earns its keep.

rule.statement: Every number in the numbers slot MUST name the system it was read from (Stripe export, server logs, GA4 report, calendar, P&L, ticket tracker) and the artefact's inputs_used MUST reference the stored evidence file or export. The freelancer MUST keep that evidence privately for as long as the case study is published; a number whose source cannot be produced on request is removed from the study.

rationale.source: FTC Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 255; widely established practice in claim substantiation

rule.rationale: A case study is a public performance claim made to sell services. When a prospect's CTO asks "how did you measure that" during the sales call, "the client told me" ends the deal; a Stripe export dated to the engagement closes it. Keeping the evidence is also what protects the freelancer if the client later disputes the number.

rule.statement: The pull-quote MUST be a verbatim sentence from a named client contact (name, role, company for the named version; role and company descriptor for the anonymised version), captured in writing (email or message) together with explicit permission to publish it, and the permission MUST be stored alongside the evidence under r-evidence-source-named-and-kept. Paraphrased praise ("the client was very happy"), composite quotes, and quotes edited beyond removing filler words are forbidden.

rationale.source: FTC Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 255 (endorsements must reflect the honest opinion of the endorser); widely established practice in testimonial collection

rule.rationale: Prospects discount marketer-written praise to zero; a real sentence from a named person with a job title carries the trust the rest of the page cannot. Written permission is what stops the study being pulled six months later when the contact changes jobs and their new employer objects to the logo on the page.

rule.statement: When the client declines a named study, the freelancer MUST produce the anonymised version with industry, company size (headcount or revenue band), geography or regulatory context, and the quoted person's role, and MUST NOT include the client name, logo, product name, unique identifiers or numbers precise enough to identify the client. The anonymised version still requires the client's written consent to the description and quote. Only a written refusal of both versions moves the engagement to a one-line internal log; a case study is never silently dropped.

rationale.source: This methodology's NDA-fallback definition; widely established practice in confidential reference selling

rule.rationale: Confidential engagements are usually the freelancer's largest and most impressive work, and without a fallback path they produce no sales asset at all. "Series-B fintech, 80 engineers, EU-regulated" keeps most of the credibility (sector, scale, numbers) while honouring the NDA; the consent requirement stops an "anonymous" study that any competitor in a 12-company niche can decode.

rule.statement: The draft MUST be written within 7 calendar days of final delivery and the study MUST be published or explicitly parked (with the reason and a revisit date) within 14 days. The artefact records the delivery date, the draft date and the publish-or-park date. Engagements more than 30 days past delivery with no draft are logged as missed and this methodology is not applied retroactively.

rationale.source: This methodology's deadline definition; widely established practice in reference collection (ask at the moment of delivered value)

rule.rationale: Memory of engagement detail decays fast and quote capture becomes impossible once the client has moved on to the next vendor. The 7-day window coincides with the client's peak satisfaction and the freelancer's peak recall; the 30-day cutoff stops a backlog of "I should write that up" from being carried for years.

rule.statement: The title MUST lead with the outcome and contain the headline number and the time frame ("How a Series-B fintech cut checkout latency 62 percent in 3 weeks"); the client name appears only in the named version. Titles that lead with the service or the freelancer ("Backend consulting for a fintech client") are rejected.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in B2B case-study and headline writing

rule.rationale: The title is the only part of the study most prospects read: on a proposal pack cover, a LinkedIn pin, or a site card. An outcome-first title with a number does the qualification work; a service-first title tells the prospect what they already know from the freelancer's profile.

rule.statement: The published study MUST end with exactly one call to action pointing at a discovery-call booking (tracked link or UTM-tagged URL), and the artefact's outcome review MUST record, at 90 days after publication, the number of discovery calls attributed to the study and whether it was included in any proposal that closed. A study with no CTA or with several competing CTAs is not published.

rationale.source: This methodology's outcome-review criterion (does the case study convert prospects to a discovery call); widely established practice in conversion tracking

rule.rationale: The study exists to book calls, and without a tracked CTA it is impossible to know whether a year of write-ups produced any. One CTA keeps the reader's next step unambiguous; the 90-day count is what tells the freelancer which engagements are worth writing up first next time.

section.title: Conclusion targets used by the decision tree

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when the engagement has a defensible number and a publishable path.

rule.statement: Skip; surface the missing precondition; do not synthesize.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when there is no measurable outcome or the client refuses both versions.
